domains.title: Abundant Jewel Princess
domains.subtitle: Sea, Transformation, and the Mother of Emperors
domains.lead: Toyotama is the daughter of the sea god Ryūjin and the wife of Hoori. Her name, 'Abundant Jewel,' evokes the treasures of the undersea palace. She is the mother of Ugayafukiaezu, making her an ancestor of Emperor Jimmu and a bridge between the ocean depths and the imperial line.

cards.name: Sea Princess
cards.desc: Daughter of Ryūjin and inhabitant of the undersea palace.

cards.name: Wife of Hoori
cards.desc: She married the descendant of Ninigi and bore his son.

cards.name: Mother of Ugayafukiaezu
cards.desc: Her son continued the line to Emperor Jimmu.

cards.name: Shape-Shifter
cards.desc: She could transform between human and sea-dragon form.

mythology.lead: Toyotama's mythology is the story of a sea princess who joins the terrestrial line but cannot stay.

myths.title: Marriage in the Sea Palace
myths.text: When Hoori descended to the undersea palace seeking the lost fishhook, Ryūjin welcomed him and gave him Toyotama in marriage. For three years they lived in the palace, and Toyotama became pregnant. Hoori longed for the land, and she agreed to accompany him.

myths.title: The Broken Taboo
myths.text: Toyotama asked Hoori not to watch her give birth. She entered a sealed hut, but curiosity overcame him. He peeked inside and saw her in her true form — a sea dragon or crocodile — giving birth. Ashamed, she returned to the sea, leaving their son Ugayafukiaezu on land. She sent her sister Tamayori to nurse him.

myths.title: Ancestor of Jimmu
myths.text: Ugayafukiaezu grew up and married his aunt Tamayori. Their son was Kamuyamato-Iwarebiko, later Emperor Jimmu. Thus the sea princess Toyotama became the mother of the imperial line's immediate ancestor.

lore.syncretism: Toyotama belongs to a widespread East Asian motif: the animal bride whose true form must not be seen. Her story parallels Chinese and Korean dragon-palace tales, but in Japan it was woven into the imperial genealogy. She also overlaps with other sea-women and dragon daughters in Japanese folklore.
lore.culturalLegacy: Toyotama is remembered as a tragic mother and a link between the sea and the imperial house. Her story appears in Noh, folk tales, and modern retellings of Japanese myth. The Ryūgū motif remains popular in Japanese art and entertainment.
lore.extendedMeditation: Toyotama is the bride who must be trusted unseen. Her return to the sea teaches that love across boundaries requires restraint. The imperial line is born from a broken promise — a reminder that even sacred genealogies carry loss.
lore.archaeology: Toyotama has no independent material cult. Her significance is textual and genealogical, preserved in the Kojiki's narrative of Hoori and the imperial ancestry.
